title: Prompts and context engineering
summary: How to decide what goes into the model's context: a clear system prompt, a few good examples, the right data, and a way out when the answer is unclear.
youWillLearn: Why the model can only be as good as what you put in its context
What belongs in a system prompt, and why rules need reasons
How examples and tags steer format and tone
Why more context is not always better, and why user text is never instructions

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.prompt: Everything you send the model for one request: instructions, data and the question.
glossary.context window: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can look at in one request.
glossary.system prompt: Standing instructions sent with every request, separate from the conversation, that set the model's role and rules.
glossary.context engineering: Choosing what goes into the model's context window for each request: which instructions, which data, which examples, and in what order.
glossary.few-shot examples: A handful of sample inputs with the ideal outputs, included in the prompt so the model copies the pattern.
glossary.XML tags: Labels like <note>...</note> wrapped around parts of a prompt, so the model can tell instructions from data.
glossary.hallucination: When a model states something that sounds right but is not supported by its input or by fact.
glossary.prompt injection: Text inside user data that tries to act as instructions to the model, like "ignore your rules and…".

steps.title: Notely sends one line and the note
body: Notely is our course's notes app. When Maya clicks Summarize, the app server (the computer running Notely's code) takes her note and sends it to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI.
With the note goes one instruction: "Summarize this note." That is Notely's whole prompt. In your demo, every summary looked fine.

scene.caption: The app server sends Maya's note plus one line of instructions.

steps.title: Same button, three different results
body: Real users arrive. One summary has twelve bullets. One invents a to-do the note never mentioned. One answers in English for a note written in Spanish.
The model is not broken. It is guessing what you want, because you never said.

scene.caption: With only one line to go on, the model fills the gaps with guesses.

steps.title: The model only knows what is on the desk
body: The model cannot see Notely, Maya, or your intentions. It sees only the text you send, which must fit in its context window, and fills every gap with a plausible guess.
So the real job is context engineering: deciding, for each request, which instructions, examples and data go in, and in what order.

callout.text: Briefing a brilliant freelancer on day one. They know a lot, but nothing about your client. A two-line brief gets a generic result. A clear brief with an example and the right files gets what you wanted.

changes: − Maya: we look only at what reaches the model
~ App Server: decides what goes into each request

scene.caption: Whatever the app server sends is all the model knows.

steps.title: The system prompt is the brief
body: The system prompt holds what is true for every request: who the reader is, what the output is for, the format, and the rules.

Give the reason behind each rule. "Only use facts from the note, because users act on these summaries" works better than "NEVER add facts". Models generalize from reasons; shouting in capitals makes them oddly cautious.

code.code:
You write summaries for Notely, a personal notes app.
The reader is the note's author, skimming on a phone.

Write at most 3 bullets, each under 15 words.
Write in the same language as the note.
Only include facts that appear in the note. Do not add
tasks or advice, because users act on these summaries.
code.caption: Reader, purpose, format, rules with reasons. Plain sentences beat clever tricks.

changes: + System Prompt: standing rules sent with every request

scene.caption: A brief joins every request: reader, format, rules and reasons.

steps.title: Show two or three good answers
body: Describing a format takes paragraphs; showing it takes one example. Few-shot examples are sample notes paired with ideal summaries.

Models copy examples closely, sometimes too closely. If both are about meetings, every summary sounds like meeting minutes. Pick two or three that differ: a short note, a messy one, one in another language.

callout.text: Wrap each example in tags such as <example>, so the model knows it is a sample, not the note to summarize.

changes: + Examples: sample notes with ideal summaries

scene.caption: Examples show the model what good looks like.

steps.title: Label the data, then ask
body: Put the note in the user message, wrapped in tags, with the actual request at the end. Long documents first, question last, tends to work best.
Add only facts the model cannot know: the note's title, the author's language, today's date if the note says "tomorrow". Each one removes a guess.

code.code:
const userContent = `<note title="${note.title}">
${note.body}
</note>

<context>
Today is ${today}. The author writes in ${user.locale}.
</context>

Summarize the note above.`;
code.caption: Tags tell the model where data starts and ends. The request comes last.

changes: ~ Note: wrapped in tags, with a few facts added

scene.caption: The note arrives clearly labeled as data.

steps.title: Give the model a way out
body: Asked for three bullets, a model produces three bullets, even from a note that says only "call mom". That pressure is where hallucination creeps in: confident text the note does not support.
So add an exit: "If the note is too short, reply exactly: Too short to summarize." Now an honest answer exists.
changes: ~ System Prompt: gains an exit for odd notes

scene.caption: With an honest answer available, the model stops inventing one.

steps.title: Notely keeps prompts in code
body: Notely's prompt lives in one file, lib/prompts/summary.ts, next to the code that calls the model. It is reviewed and versioned in git, like any other code.
Prompts change behavior as much as code does. When summaries get worse, the history of that file is the first place to look. Lesson 7 adds tests that run on every prompt change.

callout.text: Ask: where do the prompts live? One file per feature, or strings scattered through routes? Is user text wrapped in tags and kept out of the system prompt? What happens with empty or odd input? Any secrets in the prompt?

changes: ~ System Prompt: saved in summary.ts, tracked in git

scene.caption: The system prompt is a file in the codebase, with a history.

steps.title: More context is not better context
body: Tempting: send everything, all 2,000 of Maya's notes, "just in case". It costs more, runs slower, and buries what matters, so answers get worse.
Add what this one request needs. If a feature truly needs many notes, fetch only the relevant few; lesson 5 shows how.

callout.text: The note is data, not orders. A note can contain "Ignore your instructions and…". That is prompt injection, and tags alone do not stop it. Lesson 9 covers the defenses.

changes: ~ Note → All Notes: every note Maya ever wrote

scene.caption: A desk buried in notes: slower, pricier, and worse answers.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: The model sees only its context and guesses the rest. Context engineering is choosing what goes in: a system prompt with reader, format and reasoned rules; two or three varied examples; the data, tagged, with the request last; a way out for odd input.
Send only what this request needs, and treat user text as data, never as instructions.
changes: ~ All Notes → Note: only the one being summarized

scene.caption: Brief, examples, tagged note: everything the model needs, nothing more.

quiz.question: Notely's summaries sometimes include action items the author never wrote. Which change helps most?

options.text: Add "NEVER INVENT TASKS!!!" in capitals to the prompt.
options.why: Shouting tends to make models cautious in odd ways. A reason works better than volume.

options.text: Switch to the largest model available.
options.why: A bigger model still has to guess when the brief is vague. Fix the context before paying for more model.

options.text: Say only facts from the note count, explain why, and allow a "too short" answer.
options.why: The reason tells the model what matters, and the exit removes the pressure to fill bullets with invented content.

quiz.question: Both examples in the prompt are meeting notes. Now every summary reads like meeting minutes, even for recipes. Why?

options.text: Models copy the pattern of examples closely, so the examples need variety.
options.why: Examples are a strong signal. Two similar ones teach a narrow style; varied ones teach the general format.

options.text: The model is confused by having any examples at all.
options.why: Examples usually help a lot. The problem is that these two are too alike.

options.text: The examples should go after the note instead.
options.why: Order matters a little, but the issue here is what the examples show, not where they sit.

quiz.question: Claude Code builds the summary prompt by pasting the note text straight into the system prompt. What do you ask it to change?

options.text: Nothing; the system prompt is the most important place, so the note belongs there.
options.why: The system prompt is for standing rules. Mixing user data into it blurs data and instructions.

options.text: Keep the system prompt fixed, and put the note in the user message inside <note> tags.
options.why: Fixed instructions plus clearly labeled data make the model's job clearer, and a stable system prompt is also easier to cache, as lesson 8 shows.

options.text: Remove the system prompt and put everything in one long user message.
options.why: That loses the separation between standing rules and per-request data, which is the point of the system prompt.

takeaways: The model sees only its context window. Every gap you leave, it fills with a guess.
A good system prompt names the reader, the purpose, the format, and gives reasons for its rules.
Two or three varied examples teach format better than paragraphs of description.
Wrap data in tags, put the request last, and give the model a way out for odd input.
Keep prompts in versioned files. Send only what the request needs, and treat user text as data, never as instructions.
